open-question.question: What is the extension named: a name that joins Gurita and Kepala, or a descriptive one? Whichever it is, its slug is to get the direct registry lookup `ideas/gurita.md` records its own first check lacked.
open-question.alternative: Name family: descriptive, carrying the plugin's name with a qualifier. The display name is a description such as Gurita for VS Code or Gurita Missions, and the slug its lowercase form, such as `gurita-vscode`. Lookup: this mission looks the exact slug up directly on the extension registries and on GitHub, and records the dated result in the draft; the `gurita` stem is already covered by the 2026-11-10 lookup. It says what the extension is and what it serves without a sentence, is found by a search for Gurita, coins no word, needs only one narrow lookup, and leaves both Kepala and Kepalagurita untouched whatever the Kepala boundary question settles. It steps outside the head-and-arms image, so if the extension later grows into the orchestrator's interface its name does not carry over and a published name cannot be taken back. A `vscode` qualifier also reads oddly on a VS Code fork, and which registries the lookup must cover depends on the Publication venue question.

Name family: the head word already on record. The extension is named Kepala, display name and slug `kepala`, the name `ideas/kepala.md` gives the orchestrator. Lookup: this mission looks `kepala` up directly on the registries the extension could be published to and on GitHub, and records the dated result in the draft, which also discharges the lookup `ideas/kepala.md` requires before anything is published under that name. It coins nothing: the name, its meaning, and its image are already written down, and the draft's Kepala section already calls the extension's runner Kepala's transition engine with a person choosing the edge, so the extension becomes the head over the arms with no further naming work. It spends the orchestrator's name on an experiment the 2026-11-19 conversation says a deeper integration or an application of its own may follow, and an extension name once published and removed is reserved for good. It holds only where the extension is a first form of Kepala, which the Kepala boundary question decides, and if Kepala's repeated lookup fails, the extension and the orchestrator lose their name together.

Name family: the compound on record. The extension is named Kepalagurita, display name and slug `kepalagurita`, the one-word name `ideas/kepala.md` gives the whole. Lookup: this mission looks `kepalagurita` up directly on the extension's registries and on GitHub, and records the dated result in the draft. It names the extension as an interface over the whole, the head and the arms together, which fits a pane that drives every phase of a mission by buttons, and it leaves Kepala free for the orchestrator. `ideas/kepala.md` reserves Kepalagurita as an organisation or umbrella name and leaves open where it lands, so giving it to one product takes that question over. It is twelve letters, which that draft accepted only because the name would be typed rarely, and a name this broad suits an experiment poorly if a deeper integration later replaces it.

Name family: a new name in the same image. This mission chooses a third Indonesian word for a part of the octopus that joins Gurita as Kepala does, for example Mata, the eye, for the reading and watching interface, with its merged form (Matagurita) beside it. The draft records why the word fits, lists the words it ruled out with a one-line reason each, as the naming drafts do, and records a dated direct lookup of each slug on the registries and on GitHub. The extension gets a name of its own that states its role in the image, distinct from the orchestrator, so whatever the Kepala boundary question settles, neither name has to change for the other. It is a naming exercise of the size of the two naming drafts inside a mission whose subject is the extension's design: a third foreign word to explain on the landing page, no candidate on record, and short common words such as `mata` likely to be crowded on the registries, so the choice may take several rounds of lookups.

Name family: the plugin's own name, unqualified. The extension's display name is Gurita and its slug `gurita`, the extension standing as the plugin's VS Code face. Lookup: this mission looks `gurita` up directly on the extension registries, which the 2026-11-10 lookup did not cover (it covered npm, PyPI, crates.io, and GitHub), and records the dated result in the draft. Anyone who knows the plugin finds the extension under the one name they already search for, and nothing new has to be coined or explained. It names two products one thing, against the reason `ideas/gurita.md` and `ideas/kepala.md` give for a second name, that a product sitting on top of the plugin needs a name saying how it relates to it: a person installing the extension could take it for the plugin, which it does not install, and the two would be released separately under one name.

Name family and lookup: neither now. The revised draft keeps "the extension has no name of its own yet" and lists the name among the questions left for the work, with the slug's direct registry lookup due before anything is published, as `ideas/kepala.md` sets its own lookup. The name is chosen once the extension's shape, its relation to Kepala, its repository, and its publication venue are settled and its first version is about to be published, the one point at which a permanent publisher id and extension name start to matter. The goal asks the mission to settle the draft's ten questions, and this one is settled only by moving it on: the draft carries the same open question into the work, and a lookup made later may find the preferred slug taken by then.

open-question.question: From what does the mission page read whether any question lacks alternatives or a pick: the extension's own in-process parse of `open_questions.xml`, which the question view already makes, or the open-question tool's `list` filters run as a process, and in that case from which copy of the tool (one bundled in the extension as `missions.py` is, or the installed plugin's)? The recorded page state names the tool's `list` with `--without-alternatives` and `--without-recommendation` as the source, while the extension is recorded as calling no plugin tool to draw the question view, looking up no installed plugin, and bundling only `missions.py`.
open-question.alternative: The page reads the two facts from the extension's in-process parse, as the question view does, and nothing beyond `missions.py` is bundled, but the extension's tests, run as steps of the drift-gate workflow the "Extension repository home" decision already uses, run this repository's own `core/tools/open_questions.py list --without-alternatives` and `--without-recommendation` over the committed question documents (or fixtures) and fail when the parse selects different blocks. The "Mission page state" parenthetical is rewritten to name the parse, with the tool's filters named as what it is checked against. The page keeps the one-read, no-process refresh while a plugin change that moves the filters' meaning fails CI in the same commit, the same guarantee the extension's recipes and fixed lines already get from that workflow. It adds a parity test to build and maintain in the extension's suite, and the check holds only for the plugin version in this repository, not for a newer installed plugin a person runs the skills from.

The page reads whether any question lacks alternatives or a pick from the same in-process parse of `open_questions.xml` the question view already makes: a block with no `<alternative>` element counts as lacking alternatives and one with no `<recommendation>` element as lacking a pick. No open-question tool process is run and no further copy of a plugin tool is bundled, so the extension still bundles only `missions.py`. The "Mission page state" decision's parenthetical naming the tool's `list` with `--without-alternatives` and `--without-recommendation` is rewritten to name the extension's own parse, and no check ties the parse to the tool's filters. One read serves both the question view and the page label, so a refresh costs one file read and no process, and the recorded "Question document renderer" and "Live state source" decisions stand exactly as written. The two filters become a second definition outside the plugin's tested tool, and nothing catches the day the document format or the tool's selection rule moves and the label quietly disagrees with what the annotating passes would pick up.

The extension ships its own byte-identical copy of `open_questions.py` beside `missions.py`, found by the extension's own path and pinned to the same plugin version, and runs its `list --without-alternatives` and `list --without-recommendation` with `python3` on each refresh; the question view keeps its own in-process parse for drawing. The "Live state source" record that only `missions.py` is bundled is widened to both tools, and the "Mission page state" decision stands as written. The page's state comes from the plugin's own tested definition of the filters, as the live list does from `missions.py`, and the read sits naturally in the Python part the "Kepala boundary" decision keeps apart from the VS Code interface beside the state read. Two readers of one document now run side by side, the bundled tool for the label and the extension's parser for the view, so a refresh starts two more processes and the view can show a block differently from how the label counted it.

The extension runs `list --without-alternatives` and `list --without-recommendation` from the installed plugin's copy of `open_questions.py`, located per host (the fixed `~/.gemini/config/plugins/gurita` on Antigravity, `<cli> plugin list --json` on Claude Code and Codex, as `host_tests/conftest.py` finds it), with no tool copy bundled for it. The "Live state source" record that no installed plugin is looked up is amended for this one read, and the "Mission page state" decision stands as written. The label is computed by exactly the tool version the person's skills run, so it cannot drift from what the next annotating pass will find, whatever plugin version is installed. It brings back the per-host install lookup and its setup failure modes that "Live state source" was decided to avoid, and the page then reads two plugin versions at once, the bundled `missions.py` for the live list and the installed tool for the question state.

The page does not tell apart whether any question lacks alternatives or a pick: the "Mission page state" decision is amended to drop that fact, keeping `started` or `defined`, whether the question list is empty, and whether tasks remain, and the question view's collapsed rows, which already show each question's picked alternative id or no pick, are left to carry what the person needs. No source is chosen and nothing is bundled or looked up for it. The open choice disappears with no second reader of the document, no extra process, and no lookup, and the fact stays visible per question in the view the person screens anyway. It narrows a recorded decision, and a collapsed row with no pick does not say whether the block lacks alternatives or only a pick, so the page no longer shows at a glance which annotating recipe the mission is waiting on.

open-question.question: Where do the interactive command lines behind the extension's buttons come from, the `discuss-open-question` session the question view opens and any `discuss-mission-goal` session a new-mission button opens, given that `docs/ways-of-using.md` holds only headless lines and the draft has the extension hold no host flag or model name of its own?
open-question.alternative: Nothing shipped carries an interactive line. The discuss and new-mission buttons run the line the person's own recipe file holds under a fixed recipe name (one for discussing a question, one for discussing a goal), with the same placeholders filled by the interface; until that file names one, the button is shown unavailable with the recipe name it waits for. The shipped sources stay as they are. Changes no published page and adds nothing to the plugin, and the line is exactly the person's own choice of host, model, and effort, which for a conversation is the most personal setting of all; the first user, the maintainer, already keeps such lines in a file. The buttons the transcript calls the point of the extension do nothing on a fresh install, and the fixed recipe names become a contract the person must learn before the question view's discuss button or a new-mission button works.

alternative.id: Literal lines in the shipped recipe source

open-question.alternative: The interactive lines are written out literally, host binary, model, and effort included, in whatever source the shipped recipes are read from, as entries of their own: a `discuss-open-question --mission <path> <Short Title>` line and a `discuss-mission-goal <goal>` line in the interactive form (`claude "…"` with no `-p`, `agy -i "…"` on Antigravity, Codex's interactive counterpart under the legend). On the ways-of-using page that means a new section holding them, the page's opening sentence and notation widened from headless-only to cover the interactive form; in a data file or the snippet file it means entries beside the blocks. The extension fills `<path>`, `<Short Title>`, and `<goal>` and hands the line to a terminal, and a person's own recipe of the same name replaces it as the draft's recipe rule already allows. Keeps the draft's constraint whole and its one-source rule for shipped lines: the interactive lines live where every other shipped line lives, readable and runnable by hand, and the extension still holds no host flag, model name, or effort of its own. Changes a page the plugin publishes: the ways-of-using page stops being headless-only, and a line that runs nothing unattended sits among chains of complete headless invocations; where it lands depends on the shipped-recipe-source and shipped-host-lines siblings, so the docs edit cannot be written until both settle.

The extension writes no interactive line out anywhere: for a discuss button it takes a reference line of the selected recipe (its binary, model, and effort), puts the discuss skill's slash command and its filled placeholders in place of that line's prompt, and turns the headless form into the interactive one by a fixed per-host rule (drop `-p` on Claude Code, `-p` to `-i` on Antigravity, `codex exec` to `codex` on Codex). No new line has to be written or kept in step anywhere, and the conversation runs under the host, model, and effort the person already chose for the mission's other lines. Breaks the draft's constraint in a narrower form: the extension holds each host's headless-to-interactive syntax and a rule for which line is the reference, so a host changing its flags breaks the button with no published line to show what it ran, and a reference line built for a headless pass (an `xhigh` review) may be the wrong setting for a conversation.

The draft's premise is rejected for interactive lines: the extension carries a setting per host for its interactive command (binary and interactive form) and optional model and effort settings, and composes the discuss lines from those and the skill's slash command with its placeholders filled, while headless lines still come only from recipes. The button works on first install with sensible defaults and the person tunes it in the editor's ordinary settings UI, with no recipe file or published page changed. The extension holds host command syntax, model names, and effort levels of its own, which the constraint and the Recipes part rule out, and the pasted-line equivalence (a button's run is the run a typed line starts) then holds only through a composition rule the person cannot read off any page; whether composition is accepted elsewhere is the per-task line composition sibling's to settle.

alternative.id: Slash command typed into a session

open-question.alternative: No CLI line is shipped or composed for the interactive skills: the button types only the filled slash command, `/gurita:discuss-open-question --mission <path> <Short Title>` (the `$gurita:` form on Codex) or `/gurita:discuss-mission-goal <goal>`, into a terminal where the person has started a host session of their own choosing, as the snippet file's bare slash commands are used today; the extension starts no host process for it. The extension holds no binary, flag, model, or effort for conversations at all, the person's session keeps whatever host and model they started it with, and the slash commands already stand in the snippet file and the skill reference. The extension cannot tell whether the chosen terminal holds a host session or a bare shell, so the text may land in the wrong process, and the person has to start the session first; the Codex sigil still makes the typed text host-specific.

alternative.id: Slash command copied to the clipboard

open-question.alternative: The button starts nothing and types nothing: it copies the filled slash command (with the mission's path and the question's Short Title, or the typed goal) to the clipboard, for the person to paste into whatever session they use, a terminal host session or a host's own chat panel in the editor. The least the extension can do that still removes the hand work the draft names (reading the Short Title out of the XML and remembering the path), with no host knowledge, no line kept anywhere, and no risk of text landing in the wrong process. Gives up the one-click redirect to a running conversation the transcript describes, leaving a paste and a session start to the person for every discussion.

The first version of the extension offers no button that opens an interactive session: the question view's discuss button and any new-mission button are left out, the draft listing them as later work, and conversations stay in the person's own terminal as today, the question view showing the Short Title to read off. Settles nothing about interactive lines until the headless recipes and their source have been used, so no page changes and no constraint bends for a part of the flow the person spends little time in. Drops what the transcript calls most of the extension's value, the click-through to talk a question or a goal through, and leaves the person typing the longest lines (path plus Short Title) by hand; it also narrows the new-mission button sibling's options.

open-question.question: For which hosts does the extension ship command lines: the chains as `docs/ways-of-using.md` writes them (Claude Code lines, one mixed-host chain, and a legend for moving a line to another host), or each chain also written out per host?
open-question.alternative: The extension ships the chains exactly as `docs/ways-of-using.md` writes them: Claude Code lines, the one mixed-host requirements review whose review line runs on `agy`, and the legend left as documentation the person reads. No other host's form of a chain ships; a person on Antigravity or Codex moves a line by the legend's rule into a recipe file of their own. The extension holds no host flag, binary name, or prompt sigil. Nothing is written twice and nothing new is maintained: the page stays the one place a chain is written, the draft's constraint that the extension holds no host flag holds untouched, and the shipped set changes only when the page does. Out of the box only Claude Code is served: a person on another host gets buttons that run a CLI they may not have, and the hand translation the extension exists to remove comes back for them; the snippet file the maintainer actually works from already holds an Antigravity heading the shipped set would lack.

The extension ships no command lines for any host: its only recipes are the person's own recipe file, in the page's form, which the person writes or copies from `docs/ways-of-using.md` or the snippet file for whichever hosts they use. The legend stays documentation and the extension holds no host flag. The extension takes no copy of any published chain and no dependency on the page's layout, so the plugin can change its chains freely, and the maintainer, the first user, already holds a full recipe set in the snippet file. A fresh install has no buttons until the person writes a recipe file, which drops the draft's shipped-recipes part and leaves new users with the copying the extension exists to remove; it holds only if the shipped recipe source question does not settle on a shipped set.

Every chain is also written out by hand on each of the three hosts, Claude Code, Antigravity, and Codex, each line carrying that host's binary, permission flag, prompt form, and the model and effort values chosen for that host (none on Codex, which has no effort flag, and on Antigravity only the levels its models offer); the mixed-host chain stays as written beside the single-host forms. The shipped set holds one version of each chain per host, and the extension still holds no host flag of its own, only text in the lines. Every host's user gets working buttons with values tuned for that host, such as the Antigravity critical-execution case where the models `agy` runs stop at `high`, rather than the defaults a mechanical move leaves. The chains roughly triple, with nothing checking that the three forms of one chain stay the same chain, so a change to one host's form can leave the others stale; where the extra forms are written, and whether the ways-of-using page grows to hold them, turns on what the shipped recipes are read from.

The chains are written once, as the page writes them, and each chain's Antigravity and Codex forms are produced mechanically by the legend's rule (binary swapped, `--model` and `--effort` dropped, the permission flag replaced on Codex, the prompt rewritten to `'$gurita:<skill>'`) on the plugin side, by a generator or a check in this repository, so the shipped set holds every chain on all three hosts while the extension itself holds no host syntax. The mixed-host chain ships as written. Every host is served with one hand-written source and no possibility of the per-host forms drifting from it, since they are rebuilt or checked from the same lines and the same rule the legend states. The derived lines run Antigravity and Codex at their defaults with no per-host tuning, and a generator or check is new code in a repository that keeps its tooling minimal; whether there is a data file or step to hang it on turns on what the shipped recipes are read from.

The extension ships the page's Claude Code chains as written and carries the legend's rule itself: a host chosen in the extension's settings or per run makes the extension rewrite each line into that host's form at run time. This rejects the draft's premise that the extension holds no host flag, since it then holds each host's binary, permission flag, and prompt form. Every host is served from one shipped set with no extra lines written or generated, and a person switches hosts with one setting instead of maintaining recipes. The extension becomes a second copy of the legend and of each host's command syntax, which the plugin can outrun, and it revises the draft's constraint; whether it should hold host syntax at all is the same ground the per-task line composition question decides.

Every chain is also written out by hand on Antigravity beside Claude Code, the two hosts the maintainer's snippet file holds headings for, each line carrying that host's own model and effort values, while Codex gets no shipped lines and is left to the legend and a person's own recipe file. The mixed-host chain stays as written, and the extension holds no host flag of its own. It ships exactly the hosts the extension's first user works on, as the snippet file already writes them, at about two thirds of the maintenance of writing all three. Codex users, a host the plugin ships a tree for, get none of the buttons, the partition follows one person's habits rather than the plugin's host set, and the two forms of each chain still have nothing checking that they agree.

open-question.question: Where does a person's own recipe file live: inside the project as a tracked file, inside the project but untracked, or outside the project as a per-user file? The draft says only that it is a file in the recipe form, while the per-task rules are recorded as a tracked project file whose assignments refer by name to single-task lines the recipe file holds, each of those lines carrying a host, model, and effort the draft calls personal, so a tracked rule can name a line that another person's recipe file lacks.
open-question.alternative: The person's own recipe file lives outside the project as one per-user file serving every project, at a per-user path the extension reads (a default location, changeable through a VS Code user setting). A tracked rule naming a line that file lacks leaves that task's assignment unresolved: the extension shows the missing name and the loop stops at that task rather than running it under any other line. The lines stay personal and shared across the person's projects with nothing in any tree, and no task ever runs under a line its rule did not name, so a name mismatch between a project's rules and the person's file is always surfaced. A person joining a project, or a project adding a rule, stops looped runs until the person's global file gains the name, and the names are agreed by convention across projects nothing checks; whether the person can resolve the stop in place depends on the override-timing question.

The person's own recipe file is a tracked file in the project, outside every mission directory and beside the tracked rules file, so the named single-task lines are shared by everyone working in the project exactly as the rules are. A rule naming a line the file lacks is a mistake inside one tracked tree: the extension shows that task's assignment as unresolved and the loop stops at that task. The draft drops the word "personal" for these lines and says a person runs under other values only through the per-run override. Every name a tracked rule uses resolves for every person on the same commit, so the dangling-name case the question raises cannot arise between people at all, and the rules and the lines they name change together in one diff. It contradicts the draft's own finding that hosts, models, and efforts are per line and personal: a collaborator without an `agy` subscription or a Fable budget must override those tasks on every run, since the override is kept nowhere, or commit a personal preference into a file everyone shares.

The person's own recipe file lives inside the project at one fixed path the extension looks for, untracked, kept out of commits by an ignore entry the person adds (the extension writes nothing). A tracked rule naming a line that file lacks is treated as a rule that does not match: the next matching rule or the default profile applies, and only when the default profile's own line is also missing does the extension show the assignment as unresolved and stop the loop at that task. Lines stay personal and per project while being found at one known place with no setting, and a person whose file lacks a name the team's rules use still gets an unattended run under their own default rather than a stop. A missing name silently runs a task under a different host, model, or effort than the rule meant, visible only in the shown assignment; the file is lost on a fresh clone and committed by accident if the person forgets the ignore entry, which the draft cannot make the extension add.

alternative.id: Untracked in project, stop on missing

open-question.alternative: The person's own recipe file lives inside the project at one fixed path the extension looks for, untracked, kept out of commits by an ignore entry the person adds (the extension writes nothing). A tracked rule naming a line that file lacks leaves that task's assignment unresolved: the extension shows the missing name and the loop stops at that task rather than running it under any other line. Lines stay personal and per project at one known place, and no task ever runs under a host, model, or effort its rule did not name, so a missing line is always seen and fixed once in the person's file. Every collaborator must hold a line under every name the team's rules use before a looped run gets past the first task that needs it, and the file is lost on a fresh clone or committed by accident without the person's ignore entry; whether the person can resolve the stop in place depends on the override-timing question.

The person's own recipe file lives outside the project as one per-user file serving every project, at a per-user path the extension reads (a default location, changeable through a VS Code user setting). A tracked rule naming a line that file lacks is treated as a rule that does not match: the next matching rule or the default profile applies, and only when the default profile's own line is also missing does the extension show the assignment as unresolved and stop the loop at that task. The lines follow the person's own subscriptions and budgets across every project with nothing in any project tree to ignore or commit by accident, matching the draft's "personal" finding most directly, and a missing name never blocks an unattended run. Each project's tracked rules name lines in a file no project controls, so names must agree across projects and people by convention alone, and a missing name silently runs a task under a different host, model, or effort than the rule meant.

Two files: a tracked project recipe file, beside the rules file, holds a line under every name the rules use, and a per-user file outside the project may hold a line of the same name, which replaces the tracked one for that person, the replace-by-name the draft already gives a person's own recipes over the shipped set. A tracked rule naming a line the tracked file lacks is a mistake inside one tree: the assignment is shown unresolved and the loop stops at that task. Every tracked rule resolves for everyone on the same commit, while each person can still run a named line under their own host, model, and effort without committing it, so both the sharing and the personal finding hold. It adds a second recipe layer and a second file to read and explain beside the shipped recipes, and a task's actual line then depends on which per-user overrides a person happens to hold, which the shown assignment must make visible.

The revision does not settle the location: the draft keeps "a file in the recipe form" as it stands and lists where the file lives, and what happens when a tracked rule names a line the person's file lacks, as a question among its questions for the work. No choice is made before anyone has run a looped task under per-task lines, and the goal explicitly allows the finished draft to list the unknowns its decisions leave. The recorded rules and line-composition decisions leave a reference from a tracked file into a file of unknown location, so the draft describes a lookup it cannot say will resolve, and the gap is carried into the extension's work instead of closed here.

open-question.question: Does the draft adopt the 2026-11-19 conversation's new-mission button, which takes a typed goal and opens an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` session on it in a terminal, where the person carries the conversation on: as stated, in a refined form, or not at all? The draft's one way to start a mission today is the headless chain of the usage page, its `<goal>` and `<scope>` typed into an input box.
open-question.alternative: Adopted as stated: a new-mission button asks for the goal in an input box and opens a terminal running an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` session with that goal as the skill's text, where the person carries the conversation on to its proposed goal and `--at` scope and runs `/define-mission-goal` from inside the session; the draft's existing button for the headless `define-mission-goal --at <scope> <goal>` line, its goal and scope typed into input boxes, stays beside it, so the draft names two ways to start a mission. It writes the maintainer's own start of every mission (the transcript's "you click it, you write the goal, ... you will continue the conversation there") into the draft unchanged, gets the scope proposal `discuss-mission-goal` makes from the `record .` read without the person working the scope out, and keeps the one-click headless definition for a goal that is already crisp. The typed goal lands inside the interactive line's quoted prompt, so the quoting rule of "Running a line" now covers free prose of any length, and the draft holds two start buttons whose difference it must explain; the button needs an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` line to exist, which depends on how the sibling question on where interactive lines come from settles, since `docs/ways-of-using.md` holds none.

Adopted as stated for the button itself (goal typed into an input box, an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` session opened on it in a terminal, the person defining the mission from inside the session), and it replaces the draft's headless-definition button: the extension offers no button for the `define-mission-goal --at <scope> <goal>` line, `<goal>` and `<scope>` leave the placeholders the interface fills, and that line stays only on the usage page and in a person's own recipes. One way into a mission through the extension, the way the maintainer actually starts one, and the draft loses the scope input box, whose value a person typing it cold is the least placed to choose, since the definition invariant wants it as deep as the core allows and `discuss-mission-goal` is what proposes it. A person with a crisp goal and a known scope must go through a conversation, or paste the headless line by hand, to define a mission the draft's current button defines in one click, and the same quoting exposure for the typed goal and the same condition on the sibling question on interactive line sources apply.

Adopted in a refined form: the new-mission button takes no input and opens a terminal running an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` session with no text, the person typing the goal as the conversation's first turn and defining the mission from inside the session; the draft's headless-definition button with its goal and scope input boxes stays beside it. The goal is typed once, into the session that reasons over it, rather than into an input box whose text is then quoted into a command line, so no free prose of the person's passes through the line's quoting at all and the button's line is fixed text with no placeholder at all, while the quick headless definition stays available. It departs from the conversation's stated flow (type the goal, press enter, land in the terminal) by one step, and the person still meets two start buttons; it still needs an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` line from wherever the sibling question on interactive line sources places them.

Adopted in a refined form that also replaces the draft's headless-definition button: the one start button takes no input and opens a terminal running an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` session with no text, the person typing the goal there and defining the mission from inside the session, and the extension offers no button for the `define-mission-goal --at <scope> <goal>` line, which stays on the usage page and in a person's own recipes.
